summary: The run established a functional Ironclad deck and handled curse-based event rewards well, but its margin for error collapsed in Act 2. The decisive failure was combat sequencing in the final Snake Plant fight: at 2 HP, the agent spent its turn on defense and multiple debuffs while leaving a legal attack available, then died after ending the turn. Earlier HP losses also made this low-margin situation more likely.

lessons.title: At critical HP, do not spend the whole turn on redundant setup
lessons.situation: When at very low HP against an attacking enemy, especially when a lethal or high-damage attack is legal, compare killing pressure against defensive and debuff actions before committing energy.
lessons.lesson: At 2 HP on turn 3, prioritize a realistic damage race or the strongest available defense; do not spend the turn on Defend plus Intimidate plus Shockwave while leaving Pummel and multiple Strikes unused. Pummel was legal at the initial decision and remained legal after Defend and Intimidate, so it should have been evaluated before spending the remaining energy on Shockwave.
evidence_points: Turn 3 began at 2/76 HP with Snake Plant at 59/76 and intent ATTACK; Pummel, three Strikes, Defend, Offering, Shockwave, and Intimidate were all legal.
The chosen sequence was Defend, then Intimidate, then Shockwave, ending the turn with only 3 Block and no attack played.
The next logged state showed HP reduced from 2 to 0 through the subsequent death sequence, and the run ended in this combat.
lessons.reasoning: The exact incoming damage is not recorded, but the logged state shows that the chosen line produced only minimal block while consuming all energy on non-damage actions. With HP already at 2, leaving legal attacks unused created a very low-survival line; the safer reusable rule is to avoid redundant debuffs and seek lethal damage or substantially more block.

lessons.title: Treat low Act 2 HP as a healing emergency
lessons.situation: When entering a campfire or other healing decision at low HP after several damaging fights, favor recovery unless an upgrade is immediately necessary to survive the next encounter.
lessons.lesson: Do not continue an upgrade-heavy plan once consecutive fights have reduced the character to a single-digit or low-teens HP buffer. This run entered the final Snake Plant fight at 13/76 HP after ending the Centurion/Mystic fight at 7/76, so any available rest opportunity should have been treated as higher priority than another upgrade.
evidence_points: The Centurion/Mystic combat ended with HP 7/76, followed by a map move and the Snake Plant combat starting at 13/76.
The Snake Plant combat began at 13/76 and reached 2/76 by turn 3 before the run ended.
Earlier campfire decisions repeatedly chose smithing at full or near-full HP, including 74/74 on Act 1 floor 8 and 74/74 on floor 12.
lessons.reasoning: The map topology and any unavailable campfire options are not logged, so this is conditional rather than a claim that a rest was definitely available. The evidence nevertheless shows that the run maintained upgrade priority while healthy, then entered successive Act 2 fights with almost no survivability buffer; future runs should switch to healing whenever a rest is actually offered at that point.

lessons.title: Use curse-for-resource events only with a removal plan
lessons.situation: When an event offers substantial immediate value in exchange for a curse, accept it only if the deck can reach affordable removal or the reward is important enough to justify the draw penalty.
lessons.lesson: The run's event choices were effective because each curse was later removed: accept these trades when the resource gain is large and removal is realistically available, but track the future removal cost instead of treating the curse as harmless.
evidence_points: The run accepted Doubt for 175 gold on Act 1 floor 4 and then bought card removal for 75 gold on floor 6, selecting Doubt.
It accepted Parasite in exchange for healing 18 HP on Act 1 floor 11 and later bought card removal for 100 gold on Act 2 floor 19, selecting Parasite.
The final 25-card deck contains neither Doubt nor Parasite.
lessons.reasoning: Both event curses produced immediate value and were successfully removed, so this is a strategy worth repeating when removal is affordable. The important constraint is planning the removal in advance; otherwise the same event pattern would permanently worsen future draws.
